stem:
Bromocyclohexane gives mostly a substitution product with NaSH in DMF, but mostly an elimination product with {{NaOCH3}} in methanol. Explain, naming the reactions and drawing the products.
[[mol:BrC1CCCCC1]]
model:
Bromocyclohexane is a secondary halide, so {{SN2}} and {{E2}} compete and the reagent decides.
{{HS-}} is a weak base (its conjugate acid {{H2S}} has {{pKa}} 10) but an excellent nucleophile, so it attacks the carbon: mostly {{SN2}}. [[rxn:BrC1CCCCC1>NaSH;DMF>SC1CCCCC1]] {{CH3O-}} is a strong base (its conjugate acid {{CH3OH}} has {{pKa}} 15.5). It removes a hydrogen from the next carbon faster than it can reach the hindered secondary carbon: mostly {{E2}}, with a little {{SN2}} ether. [[rxn:BrC1CCCCC1>NaOCH3;CH3OH>C1=CCCCC1]] The stronger the base, the more elimination.

rubric.h: Secondary halide: both substitution and elimination are possible
{{HS-}} is a weak base and a good nucleophile: {{SN2}} named, thiol drawn
{{CH3O-}} is a strong base: {{E2}} named, cyclohexene drawn
Base strength tied to the {{pKa}} of the conjugate acids (10 against 15.5)

steps.h: The carbon that carries Br is secondary. On a secondary carbon {{SN2}} is slow but possible, and {{E2}} is possible too, so they compete.

ask.q: Why is a secondary halide the class where the reagent matters most?
ask.a: Methyl and primary favor SN2, tertiary cannot do SN2 at all. Secondary sits in between.

steps.h: The substrate is the same. Only the reagent changes: {{HS-}} or {{CH3O-}}.
{{H2S}} has {{pKa}} 10 (lecture value), methanol 15.5. Methoxide is the stronger base by more than five powers of ten.

ask.q: Which is the stronger base, and how do you know?
ask.a: Methoxide: its conjugate acid has the higher pKa.

steps.h: {{HS-}} is at the top of the lecture's table (126,000). So {{HS-}} is the better nucleophile and the weaker base: it attacks carbon.
{{HS-}}: {{SN2}}, giving cyclohexanethiol. Methoxide: {{E2}}, giving cyclohexene, with a little ether by {{SN2}}.

ask.a: Both reagents are anions that react with the halide before it can ionize.

steps.h: Stronger base, more elimination. Better nucleophile and weaker base, more substitution.

solution.answer: {{HS-}}: weak base, good nucleophile, {{SN2}}. {{CH3O-}}: strong base, {{E2}}.
solution.rule: On a secondary halide a stronger base gives more E2, and a weak base that is a good nucleophile gives SN2.

note: Lecture value for the pKa of H2S is 10. Most tables give about 7. The argument is the same with either number.

stem: Sodium ethoxide in ethanol reacts with 1-bromobutane to give mostly an ether, but with 2-bromo-2-methylpropane it gives only an alkene. Explain, naming the reactions and drawing the products.
model:
The reagent is the same strong, small base. The substrate changes.
1-Bromobutane is primary and unhindered: ethoxide can reach the back of the carbon, so the main reaction is {{SN2}}. [[rxn:CCCCBr>NaOCH2CH3;CH3CH2OH>CCCCOCC]] 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane is tertiary: three methyl groups block the back of the carbon, so {{SN2}} is impossible (relative rate 0). Ethoxide is a strong base, so it removes a hydrogen from a methyl group instead: {{E2}}. [[rxn:CC(C)(C)Br>NaOCH2CH3;CH3CH2OH>CC(C)=C]] More branching at the carbon with the leaving group means less substitution and more elimination.

rubric.h: Primary carbon is unhindered: {{SN2}} named
Ether product drawn
Tertiary carbon cannot undergo {{SN2}}: steric hindrance
Ethoxide is a strong base: {{E2}} named
Alkene product drawn

steps.h: The reagent is the same in both experiments. The substrate goes from primary to tertiary.

ask.q: What kind of reagent is ethoxide?
ask.a: A strong base that is small, so it can also act as a nucleophile.

steps.h: The flowchart for a primary halide with a non-bulky strong base: {{SN2}}. The lecture's relative {{SN2}} rate for ethyl is 0.033.
The relative {{SN2}} rate for tert-butyl is 0: steric hindrance stops the nucleophile.

ask.q: What is left for a tertiary halide and a strong base?

steps.h: The base does not need to reach the crowded carbon. It takes a hydrogen from a methyl group on the outside, and there are nine of them.
Branching slows {{SN2}} and leaves {{E2}}: primary gives mostly substitution, tertiary gives only elimination.

solution.rule: Increased branching at the carbon with the leaving group favors E2 over SN2.

stem:
tert-Butyl bromide in water gives mostly the alcohol at lower temperature. When the mixture is heated, the share of 2-methylpropene rises. Which explanation is correct?
[[rxn:CC(C)(C)Br>H2O;>CC(C)(C)O + CC(C)=C]]

choices.h: Heating produces hydroxide, a strong base, so the mechanism changes to {{E2}}
choices.why: Heating water does not make it a strong base. The lecture needed added NaOH to get {{E2}}.

choices.h: Both products come from the same carbocation. {{SN1}} is favored at lower temperature and {{E1}} at high temperature
choices.why: This is the lecture's statement: one intermediate, two fates, and heat favors elimination.

choices.h: Heating changes the substitution from {{SN1}} to {{SN2}}, which is slower, so less alcohol forms
choices.why: A tertiary carbon cannot undergo {{SN2}} at any temperature.

choices.h: At high temperature the alcohol forms by {{E1}} and the alkene by {{SN1}}
choices.why: The names are swapped: substitution ({{SN1}}) gives the alcohol and elimination ({{E1}}) gives the alkene.

steps.h: Tertiary halide, water only: no strong base, polar protic solvent. The carbocation mechanisms operate.

ask.q: Which two mechanisms share a carbocation?

steps.h: Water adds to the cation: {{SN1}}, the alcohol. Water removes a hydrogen next to the cation: {{E1}}, the alkene.
The lecture marks {{SN1}} as favored at lower temperature and {{E1}} as favored at high temperature.

ask.q: Does the base change on heating?
ask.a: No. It is water in both cases.

steps.h: No hydroxide is present, a tertiary carbon never does {{SN2}}, and the last choice swaps the names.

solution.answer: Same carbocation: {{SN1}} at lower temperature, more {{E1}} at high temperature.

stem:
Which reagent gives the largest share of elimination product with 2-bromopropane?
[[mol:CC(C)Br]]

choices.h: sodium acetate, {{CH3CO2Na}}
choices.why: Acetate is a weak base ({{pKa}} of acetic acid 4): it gives mostly {{SN2}}.

choices.h: sodium hydrosulfide, NaSH
choices.why: {{HS-}} is a weak base and an excellent nucleophile: {{SN2}}.

choices.h: sodium ethoxide, {{NaOCH2CH3}}
choices.why: Ethoxide is the only strong base here ({{pKa}} of ethanol 15.9): mostly {{E2}}, giving propene.

choices.h: sodium iodide, NaI
choices.why: Iodide is an extremely weak base ({{pKa}} of HI -10) and a good nucleophile: {{SN2}} only.

steps.h: Secondary: {{SN2}} and {{E2}} compete, and the reagent decides.
Conjugate acid {{pKa}}: HI -10, acetic acid 4, {{H2S}} 10, ethanol 15.9. Ethoxide is by far the strongest base.
A better base favors {{E2}} over {{SN2}}.

solution.rule: The strongest base gives the most elimination.

stem: 1-Bromobutane gives mostly substitution with sodium methoxide but mostly elimination with potassium tert-butoxide. Both are strong bases. Explain, naming the reactions and drawing the products.
model:
1-Bromobutane is primary: {{SN2}} and {{E2}} are the only possibilities (no primary carbocation forms).
Methoxide is a strong base but small. It reaches the back of the unhindered primary carbon: {{SN2}}. [[rxn:CCCCBr>NaOCH3;CH3OH>CCCCOC]] tert-Butoxide is about as strong a base but it is bulky, which makes it a poor nucleophile. It cannot reach the carbon, so it removes a hydrogen from carbon 2, which is easy to reach: {{E2}}. [[rxn:CCCCBr>KOC(CH3)3;(CH3)3COH>CCC=C]] The difference is size, not base strength.

rubric.h: Primary halide: only {{SN2}} and {{E2}} are possible
Methoxide is small: {{SN2}} named, ether drawn
tert-Butoxide is bulky, so a poor nucleophile
{{E2}} named, 1-butene drawn

steps.h: Primary. The flowchart: {{SN2}} with a good nucleophile or a small strong base, {{E2}} with a bulky strong base.
Both are strong bases ({{pKa}} of methanol 15.5, of tert-butyl alcohol 17). They differ in bulk.
{{SN2}} needs the oxygen to reach the back of a carbon. {{E2}} needs it only to touch a hydrogen on the outside. Bulk blocks the first far more than the second.
Methoxide: {{SN2}}, butyl methyl ether. tert-Butoxide: {{E2}}, 1-butene.

solution.answer: Methoxide: {{SN2}}. tert-Butoxide: {{E2}}, because it is too bulky to be a nucleophile.
solution.rule: A bulky strong base eliminates even from a primary halide.

stem: 2-Bromopropane reacts with sodium ethoxide in ethanol to give propene and a little ethyl isopropyl ether. Which change raises the share of propene further?

choices.h: Raise the temperature
choices.why: High temperature favors elimination.

choices.h: Lower the temperature
choices.why: This moves the balance toward substitution, the opposite of what is wanted.

choices.h: Replace sodium ethoxide with sodium acetate
choices.why: Acetate is a much weaker base ({{pKa}} 4 against 15.9): it gives mostly {{SN2}}, so less propene.

choices.h: Replace sodium ethoxide with NaSH
choices.why: {{HS-}} is a weak base and an excellent nucleophile: mostly {{SN2}}, so less propene.

steps.h: Propene comes from {{E2}}, the ether from {{SN2}}.
A stronger base, a bulkier base, a more branched substrate, a higher temperature.
Only raising the temperature is on that list. Acetate and {{HS-}} are weaker bases and better at substitution.

solution.rule: High temperature favors elimination. A weaker base favors substitution.

stem: With sodium ethoxide in ethanol, 1-bromopropane gives mainly substitution, while 2-bromopropane gives mainly elimination. Explain, naming the reactions and drawing the major product of each.
model:
The reagent, ethoxide, is a strong base and a small nucleophile in both cases. The substrate changes.
1-Bromopropane is primary: the carbon is easy to reach, so {{SN2}} is fast and wins. [[rxn:CCCBr>NaOCH2CH3;CH3CH2OH>CCCOCC]] 2-Bromopropane is secondary: the extra methyl group on the carbon slows {{SN2}} (lecture relative rates: ethyl 0.033, isopropyl 0.00083). Removing a hydrogen from a neighbouring carbon is not slowed, so {{E2}} wins. [[rxn:CC(C)Br>NaOCH2CH3;CH3CH2OH>CC=C]] More branching at the carbon with the leaving group favors {{E2}} over {{SN2}}.

rubric.h: Primary: unhindered, {{SN2}} named
Ethyl propyl ether drawn
Secondary: more hindered, so {{SN2}} is slower
Strong base then gives {{E2}}, named
Propene drawn

steps.h: Same reagent, a strong small base. The substrate goes from primary to secondary.
Ethyl 0.033, isopropyl 0.00083: one more methyl group on the carbon makes {{SN2}} about forty times slower.
The base attacks a hydrogen, not the carbon, so the extra methyl group does not get in its way.
Primary: {{SN2}}, ethyl propyl ether. Secondary: {{E2}}, propene.

solution.answer: Primary: {{SN2}}. Secondary: {{E2}}, because branching slows {{SN2}} but not {{E2}}.
solution.rule: Branching at the carbon with the leaving group favors E2 over SN2.

stem:
A student wants isopropyl methyl ether and has two plans. Plan 1: sodium isopropoxide and iodomethane. Plan 2: sodium methoxide and 2-iodopropane. Which plan gives more ether? Explain, naming the reactions.
[[mol:CC(C)OC]]
model:
Plan 1 is better.
Plan 1: the electrophile is a methyl halide. It is unhindered and has no hydrogen on a neighbouring carbon, so elimination is impossible. The alkoxide can only attack the carbon: {{SN2}}, giving the ether cleanly. [[rxn:CC(C)[O-].[Na+] + CI>>CC(C)OC + [Na+].[I-]]] Plan 2: the electrophile is a secondary halide and methoxide is a strong base ({{pKa}} of methanol 15.5). {{E2}} competes with {{SN2}} and wins, so much of the halide becomes propene and only some becomes the ether. [[rxn:CC(C)I>NaOCH3;CH3OH>CC=C + CC(C)OC]] Put the more branched group in the alkoxide and use the methyl or primary halide.

rubric.h: Plan 1 chosen
Methyl halide: {{SN2}} only, no neighbouring hydrogen, so no elimination
Secondary halide with a strong base: {{E2}} named as the competing reaction
Propene drawn as the by-product of plan 2

steps.t: Find the electrophile in each plan
steps.h: Plan 1: iodomethane, a methyl halide. Plan 2: 2-iodopropane, a secondary halide. Both nucleophiles are alkoxides, which are strong bases.
Methyl: {{SN2}} only. The alkoxide being a little bulky does not matter, because there is no hydrogen it could remove instead.
Secondary with a strong base: the flowchart gives {{E2}}. Propene forms and ether is lost.
The past exam made the same point twice: tert-butoxide with iodomethane works, and sodium cyclohexanolate with bromomethane beats bromocyclohexane with methoxide.

solution.answer: Plan 1: {{SN2}} on a methyl halide, no elimination possible. Plan 2 loses material to {{E2}}.
solution.rule: To make an ether, give the alkoxide the bulky group and use a methyl or primary halide.

stem: 2-Bromobutane gives mostly substitution with sodium azide in DMF but mostly elimination with sodium hydroxide. Which explanation is correct?

choices.h: Azide is a weak base and a good nucleophile, so it reacts by {{SN2}}. Hydroxide is a strong base, so it reacts mostly by {{E2}}
choices.why: Secondary halide: the reagent decides, and base strength tips the balance toward elimination.

choices.h: Azide reacts by {{SN1}} because it is a weak base. Hydroxide reacts by {{E1}}
choices.why: Both are anions that react with the halide directly. Neither waits for a carbocation.

choices.h: Hydroxide is the better nucleophile (16,000 against 8,000), so it should give more substitution. The result must come from the solvent alone
choices.why: Hydroxide is the better nucleophile in the table, but it is also a strong base, and on a secondary carbon the strong base eliminates.

choices.h: Azide is too bulky to remove a hydrogen
choices.why: Azide is not bulky. It does not eliminate because it is a weak base.

steps.h: Secondary: {{SN2}} and {{E2}} compete.
Azide: weak base, good nucleophile. Hydroxide: strong base ({{pKa}} of water 15.7).
Secondary, aprotic solvent, weak base and fair nucleophile: {{SN2}}. Secondary with a strong base: {{E2}}.

solution.rule: A better base favors E2 over SN2.

stem:
tert-Butyl bromide in water alone gives mostly tert-butyl alcohol. With NaOH in water, the alcohol is not formed and the only product is 2-methylpropene. Explain, naming the reactions.
[[mol:CC(C)(C)Br]]
model:
The substrate is tertiary, so {{SN2}} is impossible in both experiments.
Water alone. Water is a weak base and a poor nucleophile, so the bromide ionizes first to the tert-butyl cation. Water adds to the cation: {{SN1}}, the alcohol. A little alkene forms from the same cation by {{E1}}. Rate = k[t-BuBr]. [[rxn:CC(C)(C)Br>H2O;>CC(C)(C)O]] With NaOH. Hydroxide is a strong base. It removes a hydrogen from a methyl group in the same step in which bromide leaves: {{E2}}. Rate = k[t-BuBr][hydroxide]. This is faster than ionization, so no carbocation forms and no alcohol is made. [[rxn:CC(C)(C)Br>NaOH;H2O>CC(C)=C]] Hydroxide cannot make the alcohol by {{SN2}} either, because the carbon is tertiary.

rubric.h: Tertiary: no {{SN2}}
Water alone: carbocation, {{SN1}} named, water as the nucleophile
NaOH: strong base, {{E2}} named, hydroxide as the base
Why no alcohol with NaOH: {{E2}} is faster than ionization, and hydroxide cannot attack a tertiary carbon

steps.h: Tertiary: the possible mechanisms are {{SN1}}, {{E1}} and {{E2}}.
No strong base, polar protic solvent: the carbocation path. At lower temperature substitution ({{SN1}}) is the main result.
Tertiary plus strong base: {{E2}}. The lecture's rate data show the rate doubling when the hydroxide doubles.
It is tempting to say that hydroxide should make the alcohol faster. It cannot: {{SN2}} is blocked, and the bromide is consumed by {{E2}} before it has time to ionize.

solution.answer: Water alone: {{SN1}}. With NaOH: {{E2}}, because a strong base eliminates and a tertiary carbon cannot undergo {{SN2}}.
solution.rule: Adding a strong base to a tertiary halide switches the mechanism from SN1 and E1 to E2.

stem: 2-Bromopropane gives much more substitution with NaSH than with NaOH. A student writes four explanations. Which one is correct?

choices.h: {{HS-}} is the stronger base, so it attacks carbon harder
choices.why: {{HS-}} is the weaker base: {{pKa}} of {{H2S}} is 10 in lecture, of water 15.7. And base strength is about taking a proton, not attacking carbon.

choices.h: {{HS-}} is a weaker base than {{HO-}} but a better nucleophile, so it favors {{SN2}}, while the strong base {{HO-}} favors {{E2}}
choices.why: Both halves matter: lecture table 126,000 against 16,000 for nucleophilicity, and {{pKa}} 10 against 15.7 for basicity.

choices.h: {{HS-}} reacts by {{SN1}}, which cannot give an alkene
choices.why: {{HS-}} is an anionic nucleophile that attacks directly, and a carbocation could lose a proton to give an alkene anyway.

choices.h: Sulfur is larger than oxygen, so {{HS-}} is too bulky to reach a hydrogen
choices.why: Size down a column makes sulfur more polarizable and a better nucleophile. It is not steric bulk of the kind tert-butoxide has.

steps.h: Secondary: {{SN2}} and {{E2}} compete.
Down a column basicity falls: {{HS-}} is the weaker base ({{pKa}} 10 against 15.7).
Down a column nucleophilicity rises: {{HS-}} 126,000, {{HO-}} 16,000.
Better nucleophile and weaker base: more {{SN2}}. Better base: more {{E2}}.

solution.answer: {{HS-}} is the weaker base and the better nucleophile: {{SN2}}. {{HO-}} is the strong base: {{E2}}.
solution.rule: Nucleophilicity and basicity run in opposite directions down a column.

note: Lecture value for the pKa of H2S is 10. Most tables give about 7, which makes the same point more strongly.

stem: Each of these halides is treated with sodium methoxide in methanol. Which one gives the largest share of elimination product?

choices.h: [[mol:CI]]
choices.why: Methyl: there is no hydrogen on a neighbouring carbon, so no elimination at all. Only {{SN2}}.

choices.h: [[mol:CCCCBr]]
choices.why: Primary with a small strong base: mostly {{SN2}}.

choices.h: [[mol:CCC(C)Br]]
choices.why: Secondary with a strong base: mostly {{E2}}, but some {{SN2}} still occurs.

choices.h: [[mol:CC(C)(C)Br]]
choices.why: Tertiary: {{SN2}} is impossible, so with a strong base the only reaction is {{E2}}.

steps.h: Methyl, primary, secondary, tertiary.
Methyl > primary > secondary, tertiary none. As {{SN2}} gets slower, {{E2}} takes a larger share.
Tertiary: no substitution at all with a strong base.

solution.rule: More branching, more elimination. Methyl: none. Tertiary with a strong base: all.

stem:
1-Chloro-1-methylcyclohexane is dissolved in methanol with nothing else added. At 25 °C the main product is an ether. In hot methanol much more alkene forms. Name the two reactions and explain the effect of temperature.
[[mol:CC1(Cl)CCCCC1]]
model:
The chloride is tertiary and methanol is a neutral, polar protic solvent, so the chloride ionizes to a tertiary carbocation. Both products come from this one intermediate.
Methanol adds to the cation: {{SN1}}, the ether. [[rxn:CC1(Cl)CCCCC1>CH3OH;25 °C>COC1(C)CCCCC1]] Methanol removes a hydrogen from a carbon next to the cation: {{E1}}, the alkene. [[rxn:CC1(Cl)CCCCC1>CH3OH;heat>CC1=CCCCC1]] {{SN1}} is favored at lower temperature and {{E1}} at high temperature: high temperature favors elimination.

rubric.h: Tertiary halide, neutral protic solvent: a carbocation, the same one for both products
{{SN1}} named for the ether and {{E1}} named for the alkene
High temperature favors elimination

steps.h: Tertiary, no strong base, polar protic solvent: {{SN1}} and {{E1}}.
Ether: methanol as the nucleophile, {{SN1}}. Alkene: methanol as the base, {{E1}}.
The lecture's example is tert-butyl bromide in water: {{SN1}} favored at lower temperature, {{E1}} at high temperature. The same holds here.

solution.answer: {{SN1}} gives the ether, {{E1}} gives the alkene, and heat favors {{E1}}.
solution.rule: SN1 and E1 share a carbocation, and high temperature favors elimination.
